working: The design-token package exports TypeScript maps and three stylesheets (chat, foundation, tailwind) (packages/ui/design-tokens/package.json:8-13). It exports palette, radii, motion, typography, mobile colours, extension and VS Code variable maps and a cssVarsToString helper (packages/ui/design-tokens/src/index.ts:155,326,427,465,714,971,1074,1107).

Mobile takes its colour sets from the package (agiMobileColors, high-contrast sets, accent swatches, radii) rather than keeping its own palette (apps/mobile/src/ui/theme/tokens.ts:1-12), and its Tailwind config reads the brand scale and radii from the package (apps/mobile/tailwind.config.js:1). This is newer than the brief, which says mobile keeps its own palette.

Chrome builds its CSS variables from agiExtensionCssVars (apps/extension/src/tokens.ts:1); VS Code uses agiVsCodeCssVars as the fallback behind host variables (apps/extension-vscode/src/features/sidebar-webview/webviewContent.ts:191). All five GUI apps list @agiworkforce/design-tokens as a dependency (apps/web/package.json:37; apps/desktop/package.json:68; apps/mobile/package.json:64; apps/extension/package.json:47; apps/extension-vscode/package.json:1591).

check:css-tokens reads four surfaces (desktop, web, chrome, vscode), checks every var() reference resolves to a declared token, bans raw z-index in portal overlays, bans literal colour fallbacks in web token references, flags unused web theme colours, and checks the radius and motion ladders map to the corner and duration tokens (scripts/check-css-tokens.mjs:9-47,171-445).

The shared web library @agiworkforce/ui has about 45 primitives (Button, Dialog, Select, Sheet, Tabs, Tooltip, ConfirmAction and more) and is a dependency of Web and Desktop only (packages/ui/ui/src/primitives/; apps/web/package.json:55; apps/desktop/package.json:80).

The mobile primitive layer exists in apps/mobile/components/ui (Text, Button, PressableBox, Card, Input, Switch, Badge, Skeleton, Separator, and others). The guard scans every .tsx under apps/mobile outside that folder for raw Text, Pressable or Touchable imports from react-native (scripts/check-mobile-primitives.mjs:17-60).

The baseline of raw-control modules holds 9 entries today (scripts/config/mobile-primitives-baseline.json), counted by reading the file. The brief says 10; the file is the newer source. The baseline can only shrink: a new offender or a stale entry fails the guard (scripts/check-mobile-primitives.mjs:84-107).

One string catalogue package serves Web, Desktop and Mobile through i18next with 12 locales (ar, de, en, es, fr, hi, it, ja, ko, pt, ru, zh) and namespaces (auth, chat, common, errors, models, pricing, settings, v3, vscode) (packages/ui/i18n/locales/; apps/desktop/src/i18n/index.ts:1-8; apps/mobile/src/i18n/index.ts:13-20). check:i18n-parity compares every locale with English, including plural forms (scripts/check-i18n-parity.mjs:1-60).

VS Code now loads its messages through the shared package: it imports VSCODE_CATALOGS from @agiworkforce/i18n/vscode, which reads each locale's vscode.json (apps/extension-vscode/src/l10n/index.ts:3; packages/ui/i18n/src/vscode.ts:1-30). The brief says VS Code keeps its own locale files; the code shows the files live in the shared package.

Shared Markdown helpers exist: markdown-it plugins for math and task lists, fence classification, citation markers and highlight-language resolution in @agiworkforce/unified-chat, and normalizeMarkdownSource in @agiworkforce/utils. Chrome and VS Code both import them (apps/extension/src/features/side-panel/markdown.ts:3-18; apps/extension-vscode/src/webview/render.ts:1-13). Mobile imports the same unified-chat helpers into its own renderer (apps/mobile/src/features/chat/components/MessageContentRenderer.tsx:1-40).
incomplete: @agiworkforce/ui is not used by Chrome or VS Code, which build their own controls (apps/extension/package.json and apps/extension-vscode/package.json list no @agiworkforce/ui dependency; brief S101.30).
Chrome does not use the shared catalogue. Its strings come from the browser extension message file, read through chrome.i18n (apps/extension/src/i18n.ts:1-20).

Markdown rendering is not one implementation. Web uses MarkdownContent in unified-chat, Chrome and VS Code use markdown-it with their own wiring and sanitiser setup, and Mobile uses its own block and inline renderer (packages/ui/unified-chat/src/components/markdown/MarkdownContent.tsx; apps/extension/src/features/side-panel/markdown.ts; apps/extension-vscode/src/webview/render.ts; apps/mobile/src/features/chat/components/MessageContentRenderer.tsx). Mobile is not read by check:css-tokens (the guard lists four surfaces, scripts/check-css-tokens.mjs:11-47). Mobile colour discipline uses a separate guard, check:no-hex-mobile (package.json:397; scripts/check-no-hex-colors-mobile.mjs), which was not read in full.

established.statement: Every GUI surface takes colours, radii and type from one shared token package.
Every web-rendered surface builds UI from one shared primitive library.
Each native surface has its own primitive layer that screens use instead of raw platform controls.
Every UI surface draws its strings from one shared localisation catalogue.
Markdown and content transformations run through one shared implementation on every surface.
Each surface has a renderer for the shared content model that declares which block kinds it renders and degrades the rest (brief status: not applicable).
No hardcoded design values; design values belong to the token package.
One design system; do not invent stacks.

steps.what_happens: At build time each surface imports tokens: Web and Desktop load the three stylesheets and Tailwind theme; Mobile imports TypeScript colour maps; Chrome and VS Code turn token maps into CSS variable text with cssVarsToString.
At runtime a screen draws with primitives. Mobile Text and PressableBox come from apps/mobile/components/ui; Web and Desktop use @agiworkforce/ui.
i18next on Web, Desktop and Mobile resolves strings from bundled resources for the stored or detected language; VS Code picks a catalogue from the editor language; Chrome calls chrome.i18n.
An assistant answer arrives as text from the model or Cloud route. Each surface runs its own Markdown pipeline on the device to draw it.
In CI and locally, guard scripts read the working tree and fail on violations.

features.summary: Four shared rules for engineers. One list of analytics events and consent checks. A web start-up check that refuses bad production settings. One registry of secret patterns used for logs, telemetry and support text. A file declaring where each shared package may run, checked by a guard.

purpose.what_it_does: Defines the analytics event vocabulary and consent-gated emitter shared in packages/contracts/types; validates web server configuration at start-up and classifies every environment key; keeps one registry of secret-matching rules with named redaction policies; and declares for each shared package entry point whether it may run in universal, browser, server, native or asset contexts, with a guard on the import graph (packages/contracts/types/src/product-analytics.ts; apps/web/lib/validate-env.ts; packages/platform/utils/src/secretRedaction.ts; scripts/config/package-runtimes.json).
purpose.why_it_exists: A misconfigured production deploy, a leaked secret in a log, a server-only module bundled into a phone app, or an invented analytics event name are expensive and hard to see. Making each a shared rule with a guard stops drift. AGENTS.md section 6 requires security behaviour to fail closed and section 9 forbids silent failures (doc: AGENTS.md).
purpose.who_uses_it: Engineers and operators. Testers do not see it directly. People notice it only as a redaction marker in logs or support text, or when a bad deploy is refused.

journey: 1. Operator starts the web server. instrumentation.ts runs validateEnvironment and logs errors and warnings.
2. If errors exist in a production build and AGI_ALLOW_INVALID_ENV is not 1, start-up throws and the server does not boot.
3. A person using an app grants analytics consent. The surface's emitter queues allowed events and sends batches to the web ingest route.
4. A log, telemetry or support text passes through a redaction policy; secrets become markers.
5. Engineer adds code. Guards for config keys, security helpers and package runtimes run in the guard chain (package.json:397).

working: Web start-up validation: instrumentation.ts runs validateEnvironment in the Node runtime, logs results, records a configuration-state metric, and in production throws unless AGI_ALLOW_INVALID_ENV is 1 (apps/web/instrumentation.ts:36-63). validateEnvironment runs 15 checks including Stripe key-mode consistency, key types, the config-key registry and deployed values (apps/web/lib/validate-env.ts:1907-1925).

Stripe check: secret and publishable keys must share a mode; test-mode keys on a production deployment are an error; the message names AGI_ALLOW_INVALID_ENV=1 as the only override for an incident deployment; live keys on preview or development are also errors (apps/web/lib/validate-env.ts:319-360; apps/web/lib/__tests__/validate-env.test.ts:325-349).

Config key registry: every key web reads must be registered in validate-env.ts or recorded with a reason in scripts/config/config-keys.json. A NEXT_PUBLIC_ key whose name says it is a credential fails unless it is on a short published list (scripts/check-config-keys.mjs:19-36,92-115).

Secret registry: SECRET_PATTERN_RULES holds the patterns; SECRET_DETECTION_RULES lists those the web leak detector reads; REDACTION_POLICIES defines four policies named log, telemetry, content and evidence; redactWithPolicy applies one (packages/platform/utils/src/secretRedaction.ts:32,377,402,495). The web secret pattern list is built from this registry rather than copied (apps/web/lib/security/secret-patterns.ts:10-38). The redactSecrets function in the logger is the shared log redactor (packages/platform/utils/src/logger.ts:107).

Surfaces using the shared redactor: VS Code applies the telemetry policy (apps/extension-vscode/src/core/telemetry.ts:1-5); Chrome calls redactSecrets from the logger in its background policy and content script (apps/extension/src/background/policy.ts:2,450; apps/extension/src/content.ts:22,1238); Mobile imports it in streaming and message rendering code (apps/mobile/services/streaming.ts; found by search, usage not read).

check:security-helpers requires redactSecrets, isPathInside, sealEnvelope and openEnvelope each to be declared once and bans raw cipher calls outside apps/web/lib/crypto, with one recorded exemption for web push (scripts/check-security-helpers.mjs:19-35).

Package runtimes: scripts/config/package-runtimes.json declares 231 entry points across 56 packages: 192 universal, 28 server, 8 asset, 2 browser, 1 native (counted from the file). The guard checks each entry's static import graph and walks four client bundles (web client components, mobile app, Chrome extension, VS Code webview) so none reaches a Node built-in, server-only entry or the web crypto envelope (scripts/check-package-runtimes.mjs:3-22,168-200,340-440).

Analytics vocabulary: event names, surfaces (web, desktop, mobile, cli, vscode, chrome, api), outcomes, an allowlist of property keys, a normaliser that rejects unknown events, and two emitters (generic and account-consent based) live in one file (packages/contracts/types/src/product-analytics.ts). The server ingest route normalises each event again and drops any without account consent (apps/web/app/api/analytics/events/route.ts:25-60).

Analytics is used by more surfaces than the brief says: Web (apps/web/shared/lib/product-analytics.ts), VS Code (apps/extension-vscode/src/features/analytics/productAnalytics.ts), Chrome (apps/extension/src/features/observability/productAnalytics.ts), Mobile (apps/mobile/services/productAnalytics.ts) and the CLI, which embeds the TypeScript contract file at compile time (apps/cli/src/cloud/product_analytics.rs:9-10).
incomplete: Config validation covers only the web server; Mobile, Chrome, VS Code, Electron and the CLI validate configuration their own way (brief S101.36; the Electron, Mobile and CLI files were not opened).
The CLI has its own Rust redaction module (apps/cli/src/secret_redaction.rs:1-30) beside the TypeScript registry. Whether a test ties the two rule sets together was not found.

The brief says parity tests compare shared rules with the web copy. The parity test compares each policy's output with a recorded fixture of earlier call-site outputs (packages/platform/utils/src/__tests__/secretRedaction.parity.test.ts:1-22), and the web list now derives from the registry. Not a comparison with a separate web copy.

Mobile, VS Code and the CLI send analytics only in Cloud mode: Mobile requires appMode cloud, VS Code requires trust mode managed, the CLI requires managed privacy mode (apps/mobile/services/productAnalytics.ts:33; apps/extension-vscode/src/features/analytics/productAnalytics.ts:56-58; apps/cli/src/cloud/product_analytics.rs:20-26). Web and Chrome gates differ (cookie preference on Web; account consent on Chrome) and Chrome's mode gate was not found.
disconnected_or_disabled: The deployed-values check and rate-card check run inside validateEnvironment, but their rules were not read here (apps/web/lib/validate-env.ts:1921-1922).
not_available: Shared configuration validation on Mobile, Chrome, VS Code, Electron and the CLI (brief S101.36).

Desktop-specific analytics emitter: Desktop shows the hosted web app, so it inherits Web's; the Tauri renderer has a client failure reporting service that was not opened (apps/desktop/src/services/clientFailureReporting.ts).

established.statement: Telemetry and analytics follow one shared vocabulary and redaction path on every surface.
Configuration for every surface is validated through one shared registry and validator.
Security-sensitive helpers (crypto, redaction, path containment) live in one shared place that every surface uses.
Shared packages declare browser-only, server-only and native-only entry points explicitly.
A production deployment with test-mode payment keys is refused unless the operator sets AGI_ALLOW_INVALID_ENV=1.
Security behaviour fails closed; collect the minimum data; never commit a secret.
Do not hardcode what the repository models; no silent failures.

acceptance_criteria: Starting the web server with a test-mode payment key and VERCEL_ENV=production fails start-up; adding AGI_ALLOW_INVALID_ENV=1 lets it boot with errors logged.
Adding a process.env read of an unregistered key in apps/web fails pnpm check:config-keys.
A NEXT_PUBLIC_ variable ending in _SECRET fails the same guard.
Each redaction policy output equals the recorded fixture for the shared corpus (secretRedaction.parity test).
A server-only package imported from a Chrome, VS Code webview, Mobile or web client component fails pnpm check:package-runtimes.
An analytics event with an unknown name, bad timestamp or free-form property key is dropped by normalizeProductAnalyticsEvent, and the ingest route accepts none without consent.
Analytics events are not sent on Mobile in Local or own-key mode.
inferred: [inferred] Because the CLI embeds the TypeScript analytics contract at compile time, a contract change reaches the CLI only on its next build.
[inferred] A validator crash that is not the 'Environment validation failed' error is logged and start-up continues (apps/web/instrumentation.ts:68-72), so a bug in the validator would fail open.
proposed: [proposed] Add a test that feeds the shared redaction corpus through the CLI Rust redactor and compares markers, so the two sets cannot drift.
[proposed] Extend the config registry idea to Mobile, Chrome, VS Code, Electron and CLI, or record each as out of scope.
[proposed] Make a validator crash in production refuse start-up unless the override is set.

steps.what_happens: Web server boot: instrumentation loads validate-env and runs the checks against process environment.
On errors in production without AGI_ALLOW_INVALID_ENV=1 the boot throws; otherwise it logs and continues.
A client calls track(). The emitter checks its gate (cookie, mode, consent), normalises the event against the vocabulary, queues it and flushes in batches of up to 50.
The account-consent emitter asks the server for the consent record before sending and caches the answer for 10 minutes.
The ingest route checks CSRF, rate limit and user scope, re-checks consent, normalises each event and stores accepted ones.
Redaction runs where the text is produced: log sinks, VS Code telemetry, Chrome page text, Mobile streaming, CLI tool output.
Guards read package manifests, declared runtimes, and source imports in the working tree.

Web needs only a cookie preference, and the ingest route still needs a user scope (apps/web/app/api/analytics/events/route.ts:30). Config validation: no account.
access_and_usage.permissions: Ingest requires a CSRF token and a user-scoped database context (apps/web/app/api/analytics/events/route.ts:28-31). Operators set AGI_ALLOW_INVALID_ENV.
access_and_usage.subscription: none found in the code. No plan check appears in the analytics contract, validator, redaction or runtime declaration.
access_and_usage.limits_and_metering: Batch size is capped at 50 (packages/contracts/types/src/product-analytics.ts). The ingest route uses the default rate limit (apps/web/app/api/analytics/events/route.ts:29). Property values are cut at 120 characters.
access_and_usage.flags: AGI_ALLOW_INVALID_ENV on the web server; VS Code telemetry settings; CLI telemetry config and DISABLE_TELEMETRY or DO_NOT_TRACK variables. No feature-flag service found for these.
access_and_usage.model_compatibility: Not model dependent.
access_and_usage.provider_restrictions: none found in the code. Redaction rules are provider-shaped but do not restrict providers.
access_and_usage.local_mode: Analytics: not sent on Mobile unless appMode is cloud, on VS Code unless trust mode is managed, on the CLI unless privacy mode is managed (files cited above). Chrome and Desktop Local-mode behaviour not established. Redaction and runtime declarations: apply in Local mode; they run on the device with no payment or server call. Web config validation applies only to our hosted web server.

features.summary: A source a turn used (link, title, optional snippet) has one shape defined in the Rust protocol and generated into TypeScript. Web, Mobile and the Chrome side panel build their source records from it. VS Code parses it. Citation marker handling is partly shared and partly copied.

purpose.what_it_does: Gives every surface the same record for a web page or document an answer drew on, so source lists and numbered citation markers like [1] show consistently. features.summary: The web server (Next.js) renders pages, serves the HTTP API, and streams model answers to clients over server-sent events from one long route, sending a keepalive line after 2 seconds of silence. Desktop's chat uses this same Cloud path. Local and own-key chat do not use this route.

purpose.what_it_does: Runs the Cloud (managed) side of chat. The web app is a React app in the browser, its pages are rendered by Next.js on the server, its HTTP API is a set of route handlers, and the chat route streams a model answer back as it is written, with a keepalive so proxies do not close the connection.
purpose.why_it_exists: Cloud mode needs one server place that checks the account, plan and quota, picks a model and provider, streams the answer, and records usage. Every Cloud client (web, desktop's hosted window, extensions, CLI cloud mode) can then share one subscription system.
purpose.who_uses_it: Signed-in people chatting in the web app or in the Electron desktop window (which shows the hosted web app); the Chrome extension and other clients that call the same managed route; engineers operating the server.
problems_solved: A browser cannot hold provider keys, so a server must call the model for Cloud mode.
Long answers over HTTP need a live one-way feed and a keepalive so idle gaps do not drop the connection.
A dropped client must be visible to operators (log and failure counter) instead of silently wasting a turn.
A conversation must not be attached to a project the user does not own.
use_cases: A Premium user types a question in the web chat and watches the answer appear as it is written.
A user on the Electron desktop app chats; the window is the hosted web app, so the request goes to the same route.
A user closes the tab mid-answer; the server logs a stream_disconnected event with bytes already sent.
A user creates a conversation inside a project they own; creating one in another person's or an archived project is refused.

where_to_find_it: Web: the chat box on the signed-in web app (apps/web/app/layout.tsx:114 root layout; the composer is packages/ui/unified-chat/src/components/ChatInput.tsx).
Desktop (Electron): the same hosted web chat inside the window (apps/desktop/electron/config.ts:17 production origin; main.ts:1328 loads the entry URL).

Chrome extension: calls the managed route through its cloud client (apps/extension/src/features/computer-use/cloudAgentClient.ts:1-15 imports the managed agent helpers) [inferred: the exact side-panel label was not read].
Mobile, VS Code, CLI: whether their Cloud mode reaches this exact route was not established (see unknowns).
prerequisites: A signed-in account: the route's auth gate uses the Clerk identity helper (apps/web/app/api/llm/v1/chat/completions/lib/auth-gate.ts:6) and also accepts an API key (route.ts:1481-1483).

A plan or free allowance that admits Cloud chat: Free users go through the free-quota lanes (route.ts:1489-1509); capability 'managed_chat' lists Free-through-Enterprise tiers (packages/contracts/types/src/billing-catalog.ts:350) [inferred from CLOUD_CHAT_TIERS name; list not fully read].
Network access to the server.
screens_and_controls: Message box and send control in ChatInput (packages/ui/unified-chat/src/components/ChatInput.tsx:173 onStop prop; the send button doubles as the stop control, line 1024 comment).
No separate UI for the heartbeat; it is a transport detail.
journey: 1. The person types a message and sends it.
2. The client calls the chat completions route (public alias /v1/chat/completions rewritten to /api/llm/v1/chat/completions, apps/web/lib/api-host-route-contract.ts:3-4).
3. The server checks sign-in, rate limit, terms and subscription, then dispatches the turn (route.ts:1475-1515).
4. The answer streams back as text/event-stream; the person sees words appear.
5. If nothing is written for 2 seconds the server sends a ': keepalive' comment line (sse-heartbeat.ts:6, :29).
6. The stream ends and the answer is saved; leaving the page early drops the connection and the server logs it.
feedback_and_outputs: Streamed answer text.
Response headers such as X-AGI-Resolved-Model, X-Quota-Warning and X-AGI-Tool-Loop (route.ts:1195-1235 area; baseAgentHeaders at route.ts:~905-935).
On refusal or failure the route returns an error response; the brief describes no automatic retry of a dropped stream.
settings: Server environment: AGI_DURABLE_INITIAL_TURNS (kill switch for detachable turns, apps/web/lib/workflows/durable-initial-turns.ts:6).
No per-user setting for the heartbeat was found (none found in the code).

working: Next.js 16 web app: root layout is an async server component (apps/web/app/layout.tsx:114); Providers.tsx starts with 'use client' (apps/web/app/Providers.tsx:1); a public share page builds metadata on the server (apps/web/app/shared-artifact/[token]/page.tsx:50-58); next ^16.4.5 (apps/web/package.json:148).
Chat route allows 300 seconds per request (apps/web/app/api/llm/v1/chat/completions/route.ts:161) and is exported through CORS, rate-limit and error wrappers (route.ts:1526).
Heartbeat wrapper: 2000 ms interval, keepalive comment line, SSE headers with X-Accel-Buffering no (apps/web/app/api/llm/v1/chat/completions/lib/sse-heartbeat.ts:6-12, :29).

Client-drop detection: cancel before the source ends records a failure counter 'stream_disconnected' and logs event 'sse_stream_disconnected' with bytesDelivered, elapsedMs and reason (sse-heartbeat.ts:23-26).

Plain (non-tool) chat is streamed by stream-transform and wrapped with the heartbeat (lib/stream-transform.ts:956-972); an aborted client settles the stream as cancelled and saves the partial answer (stream-transform.ts:737-750).
Conversation creation checks that a given project belongs to the user, is not archived and not deleted, else returns 'Project not found' (apps/web/app/api/chat/conversations/route.ts:236-250).
A temporary chat cannot be placed in a project (route.ts:231-233).
incomplete: The brief gives only one platform status and no per-app status; per-app reach (mobile, VS Code, CLI) is not confirmed (unknowns).

No retry of a dropped stream is described in the brief; the code path for plain chat has no reattach (not handled in the code for plain request-scoped turns). Detachable turns can be followed through the run journal (see F102-02).
disconnected_or_disabled: Detachable (durable) turns are switched off by AGI_DURABLE_INITIAL_TURNS being 0, false or off (durable-initial-turns.ts:6-14); then turns run request-scoped and end with the connection.
not_available: Local and own-key (BYOK) chat never reach this route (apps/web/app/api/llm/v1/chat/completions/lib/request-processor.ts:4876 comment).

Desktop (Electron) has no on-device chat: the dispatcher refuses local-inference commands with 'AGI Desktop answers every conversation in the cloud' (apps/desktop/electron/runtime/dispatcher.ts:3236-3244).

established.statement: The web app runs as a client-side React application in the browser.
Pages are rendered on the server by Next.js server components.
A backend HTTP API runs as Next.js route handlers.
Model output streams to clients over SSE with heartbeats from a long-lived route.
Desktop chat is Cloud only; on-device inference is refused in the Electron shell.

acceptance_criteria: With a valid sign-in, POST to the chat route returns Content-Type text/event-stream and words arrive before the stream ends.
When the model is silent for more than 2 seconds the stream contains a ': keepalive' line.
If the client cancels mid-answer, the server logs event sse_stream_disconnected with a bytesDelivered number and increments the stream_disconnected failure counter.
Creating a conversation with a projectId of another user's, an archived or a deleted project returns a not-found error and creates no row.
A turn with no sign-in is refused before any model call.
A Free-plan user's chat is served through the free lanes and never bills a paid reservation [inferred from route.ts:1489-1509].
inferred: Every Cloud client should show a visible provider/mode label so a Local or own-key chat is never silently sent here (AGENTS.md section 6 requires explicit consent for crossing).
proposed: [proposed] Add per-app status rows to the brief so reach on mobile, VS Code and CLI is recorded.
[proposed] Expose the heartbeat interval as configuration if operators need to tune proxies (today it is a constant, sse-heartbeat.ts:6).

steps.what_happens: The browser (or desktop window) sends the message to the chat route.
The server authenticates, rate-limits, checks terms and subscription, takes a turn slot and dispatches.
Free users are first tried on free-quota lanes; a refusal may be retried by the fallback lane.
The request is validated and a provider adapter is chosen from the adapter table; an unlisted provider is an explicit failure.
The adapter calls the model provider and the answer is converted to SSE chunks.
The stream is wrapped with the heartbeat; a keepalive is enqueued after 2 s of silence; a cancel before the end is logged as a client drop.
Usage is settled (success, failure, or cancelled with the partial answer saved).

features.summary: Agent turns that use tools or AGI Work, and approved deep-research runs, start as durable Workflow runs so they can outlive the browser request. A reaper cron ends runs whose worker vanished. If the durable path fails, the turn degrades to a request-scoped stream. Deep Research needs Premium or above.

purpose.what_it_does: Runs long Cloud agent turns as durable workflows. The run is journaled, can be followed again, can be cancelled, can wait for a sleeping desktop, and is cleaned up by a reaper if its worker is lost. Deep Research is a bounded loop of plan, search, fetch and report.
purpose.why_it_exists: A normal HTTP request dies when the tab closes. Agent and research turns take minutes and cost money, so they must survive disconnects, settle usage exactly once, and never leave a run stuck forever.
purpose.who_uses_it: Paid users running tool turns, AGI Work or Deep Research on the web or any client that starts a Cloud agent turn; operators who watch the reaper.
problems_solved: Turns lost when the browser closes.
Runs stuck in a working state that block a conversation.
Device-based steps when the desktop is asleep.
Paying for a turn nobody sees.
use_cases: A Premium user turns on Research for a question, closes the tab, and returns to a finished cited report.
A user starts an AGI Work task and stops it from the chat; the server records the cancellation and the run ends.
A run whose worker crashed is ended with a plain message by the reaper within about 18 minutes.
A task that needs the user's desktop waits up to 60 minutes for it to wake, then continues without device tools.

journey: 1. The user sends a tool turn, an AGI Work task or a Research turn.
2. The server creates a run row and tries to start the durable workflow (route.ts:946-990).
3. The first stream frame must arrive within a budget or the durable start is cancelled and the turn runs request-scoped (route.ts:967-980).
4. The workflow loops: wait for a device if needed, run one invocation, repeat until terminal, settle the work plan, close the stream (cloud-agent-workflow.ts:69-100).
5. The user may close the tab; the run keeps going and its events are kept in the run journal.
6. The user may stop the run: POST to the run route marks cancellation; the workflow notices it.
7. The final answer or report appears; a stuck run is ended by the reaper.

Deep research loop: defaults 6 iterations, 12 searches, 3 parallel tool calls; 8 fetches total and 3 per round; plan up to 6 queries and 3 questions (research-loop.ts:178-232); fetch step near line 2767; report cost settled by job 'research.settle-report-cost' (job-handlers.ts:~360).

steps.what_happens: The route classifies the turn and creates a run row.
The server starts the workflow with a 10 s deadline and attaches the run to the workflow run id.
The workflow runtime (Vercel Workflow) executes steps and keeps durable state.
Each invocation calls the model provider through the tool loop, using tools, connectors and optionally the user's device.
If a device step is needed the workflow waits for the desktop (up to 60 minutes).
The result is settled; the work plan is settled; the stream is closed.
The reaper cron ends runs with no update beyond the age limit and cancels their workflow runs.

features.summary: Server-side background work: a cron drains queued jobs (media, file purge, exports, email, webhooks); a cron fires due scheduled runs; uploaded documents are indexed by durable workflows with a retry sweep. Workers that sync mail or drive content on a schedule do not exist.

purpose.what_it_does: Runs work that is not part of a web request: queued jobs with retries and dead letters, scheduled agent runs, search indexing of uploaded knowledge files, and large chat-file intake.
purpose.why_it_exists: Slow or retried work must not block a request, must survive crashes, and must be metered. Scheduled tasks must run when the user is away.
purpose.who_uses_it: Users who upload project files, schedule tasks, request exports or generate media; operators who watch queues.
problems_solved: Uploads that need chunking and embedding.
Retrying failed emails, webhooks and deletions with backoff.
Running a user's saved prompt at the time they chose.
Detecting a queue that stopped draining.
use_cases: A user adds a PDF to a project and later finds it searchable.
A user with a paid plan schedules a daily summary; the cron runs it.
A user requests a data export; a job builds the archive and emails when ready.
Nothing syncs a user's mailbox content in the background; Gmail changes only fire event triggers.

journey: 1. The user uploads a document or creates a schedule.
2. For a document, the server dispatches an indexing workflow; if the start fails the document stays pending (project-knowledge-files.ts:105-123).
3. Every 10 minutes a cron reserves due documents and starts workflows (vercel.json:62; index-retrieval-documents/route.ts).
4. For a schedule, the 15-minute cron claims due runs in waves of 10 for up to 55 s (run-schedules/route.ts:14-18).
5. Each run executes the saved prompt through the managed agent path and records success, failure, timeout or cancel.
6. Every 5 minutes the drain cron claims and runs queued jobs (vercel.json:150).
feedback_and_outputs: Index state on knowledge files; keyword-only note when embeddings fail ('The embedding provider did not respond; keyword search still works and indexing retries automatically.', retrieval-index-service.ts:118).
Schedule run history, completion notifications and email (job kinds notifications.schedule-completed, email.schedule-completed, job-handlers.ts:347-367).
Quota message: '<plan> plans do not include scheduled tasks. Upgrade to schedule unattended runs.' (schedule-service.ts:884-889).
settings: AGI_DB_LOW_POWER skips these crons after minute 15 each hour (cron-low-power.ts:3-17).
CRON_SECRET (name only) authenticates cron calls, minimum length 32 (apps/web/lib/server/cron-auth.ts:19).
Missed-run policy per schedule: run_once or skip (schedule-service.ts:2102 area).

working: Drain cron: budget 250 s, at most 12 jobs in flight, handlers for webhooks, notifications, email, deletion, file purge, research settlement, event triggers, image generation and data export (apps/web/app/api/cron/drain-background-jobs/route.ts:17-18, :35-36; apps/web/lib/jobs/job-handlers.ts:347-367). Per-queue concurrency, attempts, backoff, lease and retention are in JOB_QUEUE_POLICIES (apps/web/lib/jobs/job-queues.ts:18).
Drain reports queue depth and age, reaps expired leases, and pages operators when a queue is not draining (apps/web/lib/jobs/job-drain.ts:209 and helpers).
A failed drain returns HTTP 500 (drain route:43-49).

Scheduler: waves of 10, 40 s per wave, 55 s sweep, up to ceil(50/10) waves (run-schedules/route.ts:14-20; PLATFORM_SCHEDULE_RUNS_PER_SWEEP=50 at billing-catalog.ts:478); each wave first expires lapsed approvals and recovers expired claims, then claims due runs (schedule-service.ts:2471-2500).
Scheduled runs use the managed route with a usage reservation and managed-compute access check (scheduled-agent-executor.ts:12-14, :98, :110).

Indexing: dispatch on upload/reindex, 10-minute cron sweep, durable workflow with one step that chunks, embeds (metered), and stores chunks; embedding failure leaves keyword-only chunks and retries (retrieval-index-service.ts:658-780; start-retrieval-index-workflow.ts:32-50).
Large chat-file intake runs as its own workflow with a 5-minute sweeper (chat-file-intake-workflow.ts; vercel.json:66).
Video generation has its own workflow (apps/web/lib/workflows/video-generation-workflow.ts).
Gmail: a webhook and a watch-renewal cron feed event triggers (apps/web/app/api/webhooks/gmail/route.ts; lib/triggers/gmail-watch.ts:492; vercel.json:198).
incomplete: The scheduler cron has maxDuration 60 s (run-schedules/route.ts:12), so one sweep can leave runs due; it logs 'Scheduled-task sweep ended with schedules still due'.

features.summary: Cloud code runs in an isolated remote sandbox, but only when the server cutover flag AGI_E2B_EXECUTION is 1, a sandbox key and a compute price are set, and the plan includes AGI Code (Basic or above). A cloud browser and a cloud virtual computer do not exist; the cloud browser is declared unavailable.

purpose.what_it_does: Provides managed isolated sandboxes where the model runs code and where coding sessions run, billed by compute seconds. It also records that a cloud browser and a cloud computer are not built.
purpose.why_it_exists: Running untrusted code needs isolation, metering and limits. Users without a local setup still want code execution in the cloud.
purpose.who_uses_it: Paid users of AGI Code on the web and users whose chat uses the code-execution tool; operators who enable the sandbox.
problems_solved: Running generated code safely away from the user's machine.
Charging for sandbox seconds and refusing when no price exists.
Keeping credentials out of the sandbox (egress proxy rules).
use_cases: A Basic user opens a Code session on the web and runs a repo task.
A chat turn runs a Python snippet in the sandbox when the execution tool is on.
On a deployment where the flag is off, the code session is refused with 'Managed Code is not enabled for this deployment. Use the desktop app for local code.'
A user asking the agent to drive a cloud browser gets the built-in browser or the user's own Chrome instead.

where_to_find_it: Web: the Code workspace at /code and /code/[sessionId] (apps/web/app/code/[sessionId]/page.tsx); '/code/computer' titled 'Your computer · Code' sends tasks to the user's own computer, not a cloud computer (apps/web/app/code/computer/page.tsx).
Desktop: coding sessions run locally (see F102-05, F102-06).
Visible entry label on the web nav: unknown.
prerequisites: Signed-in account.

A plan that includes AGI Code: sandbox count above 0 and a coding-agent daily budget above 0 (billing-catalog.ts:836-839 planIncludesAgiCode); Free has 2 sandboxes but budget 0, so it does not include Code. basic and above do (budget 100 cents/day for basic).
Server: AGI_E2B_EXECUTION=1, E2B_API_KEY set and a priced compute rate (apps/web/lib/e2b/gate.ts:20-28).
Managed compute private beta not switched off (AGI_MANAGED_COMPUTE_PRIVATE_BETA; default on, apps/web/lib/managed-compute-gate.ts:55-58).
screens_and_controls: Code session creation (POST /api/code/sessions), network access choice (Isolated, Trusted hosts, Full internet) and extra hosts; full internet refused while credentials would enter the sandbox (cloud-code-session-open.ts:62-100).
journey: 1. The user starts a Code session.
2. The server checks the deployment gates, workspace policy, managed-compute access and plan.
3. The server provisions a sandbox after reserving compute funds.
4. The user or agent runs code; output returns.
5. Idle sandboxes are reclaimed by a cron (vercel.json:54).

Use Local or BYOK in the meantime, or try again shortly.'; 'Your plan does not include managed Code sessions' (cloud-code-session-service.ts:1245).
Code-run route says 'Running code is not available on this deployment.' (chat code-runs route.ts:76).

Session open refuses when provisioning is not ready or beta is off, then checks egress rules, harness credentials, workspace gates, managed compute access and plan (cloud-code-session-open.ts:37-200).
Runtime fails closed: refuses to provision without a compute rate or funds reservation (apps/web/lib/e2b/runtime.ts:801, :886, :941).

Chat tool loop returns 'Tool ... is not available.' for execution tools when the cutover is off (apps/web/app/api/llm/v1/chat/completions/lib/tool-loop.ts:2802-2808); code-runs route answers service unavailable (apps/web/app/api/chat/conversations/[id]/code-runs/route.ts:76).

The product runs a virtual computer in the cloud that the agent can operate. Status: missing.
Sandbox compute must be priced; provisioning fails closed otherwise.

acceptance_criteria: With AGI_E2B_EXECUTION unset or 0, opening a Code session returns the 'not enabled for this deployment' error.

The cloud browser capability reports available false with the stated reason.

proposed: [proposed] Turn the sandbox on in production once pricing is configured, as the brief says.
[proposed] Decide whether the cloud browser and cloud computer are on the roadmap; the contract already reserves a 'cloud' browser session kind.

features.summary: The Electron desktop app is a window that loads the hosted web app, with a locked-down bridge to a main process that serves native commands through a dispatcher after folder and capability checks. For coding sessions it starts the bundled CLI in app-server mode, which hosts local MCP tool servers. Desktop chat itself is Cloud only.

purpose.what_it_does: Shows the hosted web app in an Electron window, gives it a permission-checked bridge to the user's files, shell and coding runtime, and starts the AGI CLI as a long-running helper for coding sessions in an approved folder. That helper starts MCP servers as local child processes.
purpose.why_it_exists: The desktop must feel like one product with the web while doing things a browser cannot: touch local folders, run commands, host local tools.
purpose.who_uses_it: People who install the AGI desktop app on macOS (and other platforms the packaged app supports); developers running local coding sessions.
problems_solved: One UI for web and desktop without a second front end.
Safe access to local folders: nothing runs before the user grants a folder and a capability.
Long-running coding agents with their own process and recovery.
Local tool servers (MCP) with a cleaned environment.
use_cases: Open the desktop app and land in the hosted sign-in or chat.
Add a folder under Settings, then start a coding session that runs the CLI helper in it.
Add a local MCP server and test it.
The window crashes; the app reloads it once, then shows a crash screen.

where_to_find_it: Desktop app window (Electron).

Settings, Capabilities page, section 'Local access' with 'Folders' ('Add a folder', 'Reveal', 'Remove') and 'Commands' (apps/web/features/desktop-host/components/LocalAccessSection.tsx:37-64; apps/web/features/settings/sections/CapabilitiesSection.tsx:213; nav label 'Capabilities' in WebSettingsModal tests).
Section 'Developer' with 'Local MCP servers', 'Add server', 'Edit config', 'Test', 'Tools', 'Remove' (apps/web/features/desktop-host/components/LocalMcpSettings.tsx:34-48).
Not shown on web, mobile, CLI-only, VS Code or Chrome (the host section returns nothing without a desktop host: LocalAccessSection.tsx:~393 'if (!host) return null').
prerequisites: Install the desktop app and sign in through the hosted page.

For coding sessions and MCP: approve a folder first ('Approve a folder for coding sessions first. MCP servers run through the AGI CLI, which starts in an approved folder.', LocalMcpSettings.tsx:41-42).
Grant the capability (shell.execute) when asked.
screens_and_controls: Native approval dialogs for capabilities and MCP launches (apps/desktop/electron/runtime/mcpApprovalReview.ts).
Crash screen after repeated renderer faults (main.ts:895-915).
journey: 1. The user opens the app; the window loads the hosted entry URL (main.ts:1328) after the app is reachable (main.ts:326).
2. The user signs in; sign-in screens and the persistent session partition keep the session (config.ts REMOTE_SESSION_PARTITION).
3. The user adds a folder; the main process stores consent (workspaceStore).
4. The user starts a coding session; the main process spawns the CLI with app-server and consent arguments (developerSessionService.ts:1453-1470).
5. The user adds an MCP server; the helper starts it when needed; project servers need approval first.
6. If the window dies the app reloads once; a second quick fault shows a crash screen.
feedback_and_outputs: Native question dialogs with the exact command or launch details.
Messages such as '<folder> is no longer on this Mac, so no coding session can run in it.' (developerSessionService.ts:~1426-1430).
Shell and runtime events streamed to the web UI through the runtime event channel.
settings: CLI binary: a custom path chosen in Settings, else the bundled CLI, else an installed one, else 'agi' on PATH (developerSessionService.ts:373-381).
AGI_CLOUD_APP_ORIGIN is honoured only in an unpackaged build (config.ts:~62-72 cloudAppOriginFrom).
Programs allowed or blocked (F102-06).

working: Window loads the hosted app; the API base must be first-party HTTPS or localhost without credentials (apps/desktop/electron/config.ts:46-50, cloudAppOriginFrom ~line 62); packaged builds ignore the environment override.
Window security: contextIsolation on, sandbox on, nodeIntegration off, preload bridge, persistent partition (apps/desktop/electron/main.ts:1103-1115).

Bridge calls require a trusted sender and go to dispatchDesktopRuntime (main.ts:423, :525-540). The dispatcher refuses local-inference commands, then classifies every command into session, folder or ungated, and refuses a command found in none or two tables (dispatcher.ts:3326-3365).
Folder capabilities: each folder command names a capability with a plain reason and the user is prompted once (dispatcher.ts:640-720, :3280-3320).

Helper: spawned detached with app-server; for the bundled signed CLI it also passes workspace-consent arguments and a worktrees root; SSH environments use a remote launch (developerSessionService.ts:1431-1470). Its environment is the app's with guard-lifting variables removed plus the cloud origin (developerSessionService.ts:1182-1191). Stopping closes stdin then kills the process group after a grace period (developerSessionService.ts:~636-668).

MCP host: the CLI uses the agiworkforce-mcp crate; local stdio servers are child processes with piped stdin, stdout and stderr, an emptied environment plus an allowlist, and manifest variables that would load code are refused (crates/agiworkforce-mcp/src/transport/stdio.rs:447-470). The client also supports HTTP and SSE transports (client.rs open_conn ~line 1087).
MCP management commands (list, add, remove, enable, test, tools, logs, approval review) are dispatcher commands that need shell.execute (dispatcher.ts:845-900, cases ~2862-2890).
Crash recovery: a renderer that is gone or unresponsive reloads once, then shows a crash screen with a reference (main.ts:895-915; runtime/rendererRecovery.ts:63).

features.summary: Commands that run on the user's computer are started as programs, not through a shell, after a program allow or block check and an approval. On macOS they run inside Seatbelt, on Linux inside bubblewrap when installed. With no sandbox the desktop asks every time. The CLI has its own sandbox and warns when it is off.

purpose.what_it_does: Runs local commands for a hosted agent (through the desktop) and for coding sessions (through the CLI), inside a sandbox that limits writes to the approved folder and blocks the network unless allowed. Long or interactive programs run as background commands with a terminal.
purpose.why_it_exists: An agent that can run programs can damage the machine or leak data. The sandbox, allow list and approvals limit what a command can reach.
purpose.who_uses_it: Desktop users whose cloud agent has device tools, developers in coding sessions, CLI users.
problems_solved: Unreviewed commands changing files outside the folder.
Secrets in the environment leaking to a command.
Commands blocking forever or flooding output.
Account switching programs.
use_cases: The cloud agent asks to run a test command in an approved folder; the user sees the exact command and chooses Run once.
The user adds git to the allowed programs so it runs without asking.
A dev server is started as a background command and its output read later.
A CLI user runs a command in the workspace sandbox with the network denied.

where_to_find_it: Desktop approval dialog 'Run a local command?' with buttons 'Cancel' and 'Run once', and a checkbox 'Allow network access for this command' (apps/desktop/electron/runtime/dispatcher.ts:1984, :1999-2025).
Without a sandbox the dialog is 'Run without a sandbox?' with 'Run without a sandbox' (dispatcher.ts:2038-2050).

journey: 1. The agent proposes a command.
2. The desktop parses it into a program and arguments; pipes, redirects and variables are refused.
3. Policy: always-refused programs and the blocked list are denied; allowed names run; others ask.
4. If asked or no sandbox exists, the dialog quotes the folder and exact command.
5. The command runs in the sandbox with a cleaned environment and a private scratch folder.
6. Output streams; the run ends on exit, timeout, size cap or cancel.
feedback_and_outputs: Streamed stdout and stderr, exit code, signal, truncated and timed-out flags, duration (shellService.ts:~810-830).

Refusal messages such as 'Local commands run without a shell, so ... cannot be used...' and '<program> did not run. This computer has no sandbox for local commands, and running it without one was not approved.' (shellService.ts:567-575, :613-618).
settings: Allow and block lists stored on the device (desktop-shell-policy.json in user data, shellPolicyStore.ts).
CLI: --no-sandbox, organization-forced sandbox, scrub environment settings (sandbox.rs:596-640).

working: Parse and policy: control characters refused; argv parsing; always-refused programs; blocked then allowed lists; a program named by path asks even if allowed (packages/contracts/local-runtime/src/shell.ts:237-274; shellService.ts:554-620). Limits: command 4000 chars, input 4000 chars, output 1,000,000 bytes, default timeout 120 s, max 600 s (shell.ts:44-48).
Sandbox detection: macOS uses /usr/bin/sandbox-exec; Linux uses bwrap found on PATH; every other platform gets backend none (apps/desktop/electron/runtime/shellSandbox.ts:22, :189-203).

Sandboxed spawn: writable roots are the pinned project folder plus a private scratch folder; protected host paths such as the app's own data are read-only and unreadable; network denied unless the user ticks the box (shellService.ts:554-680; dispatcher.ts:2387).
No sandbox: every run asks, allowed or not, with a full-account warning; refusal ends with sandbox-unavailable (shellService.ts:585-620; dispatcher.ts:2038-2050).
Environment: only an allowlist of variables passes (shellService.ts:220-290).
Run: spawn without a shell, detached process group, timeout kill, output cap, streamed chunks (shellService.ts:686-820, KILL_GRACE_MS 2 s at :104).

Background and terminal commands: macOS runs them through /usr/bin/script for a terminal; reading, typing (each input approved) and stopping are supported (shellService.ts:139, :953-1070). No PTY library was found in this file; the terminal is `script` on macOS only; on other platforms background commands are plain pipes [inferred from the `terminal = process.platform === 'darwin'` line, shellService.ts:~965].

Server-side review: tool calls can carry a 'review' text that forces approval even for allowed programs (shellService.ts:~98-102; dispatcher.ts:2074 serverReview); the web device tool schema asks the model to set it for payments, messages, deletes, security changes and passwords (apps/web/lib/device-steps/device-tools.ts:53-58). The shellService comment says the server sets it once a turn has untrusted content; the setting code for that was not found, so both statements are recorded.

CLI: SandboxType detects Seatbelt or bubblewrap (apps/cli/src/sandbox.rs:188-217); run_command uses the workspace sandbox, background option, network policy, internal destination refusal (apps/cli/src/features/exec/tools/bash/mod.rs:70-115); disabled() prints 'warning: running without OS-level sandboxing, system commands will have unrestricted access' (sandbox.rs:~455-462); --no-sandbox is honoured only when the organization has not forced the sandbox and the workspace is trusted (sandbox.rs:612-618).
incomplete: Windows has no sandbox in either app: detectShellSandbox returns none and the CLI detect returns None off macOS and Linux (shellSandbox.ts:189-203; sandbox.rs:196-217).
The brief says Seatbelt or Landlock; no Landlock backend exists, Linux uses bubblewrap (crates/agiworkforce-sandbox-policy/src/wrap.rs:36-39 lists only MacosSeatbelt and LinuxBubblewrap).
disconnected_or_disabled: The CLI sandbox can be disabled by --no-sandbox in a trusted workspace (sandbox.rs:596-618).
not_available: Pipes, redirects and variable expansion in desktop local commands (shellService.ts:567-575).
Sandbox on Windows.

features.summary: The AGI command-line app. Started with no prompt in a terminal, it opens a full-screen interactive screen, or a plain line-based session when asked. Given a prompt, piped text or images, it answers once and exits, as plain text, raw text, JSON or streaming JSON lines, which suits scripts and CI.

purpose.what_it_does: The CLI (binary 'agi', plus a second binary 'agiworkforce') is a terminal coding agent. It has two ways to run. Interactive: a full-screen terminal screen (built with ratatui) or a classic line-based session. One-shot: it takes one prompt, runs the agent to the end of the turn, prints the result and exits (apps/cli/Cargo.toml:15-21, apps/cli/src/lib.rs:8143-8330).
purpose.why_it_exists: Developers need the same agent in a terminal and in scripts. The product requirements list the CLI as the developer engine and terminal agent, with user command 'agi' (doc: docs/product/requirements.md:66, :82). The desktop and VS Code extension also reuse the CLI as their local runtime (apps/desktop/electron/runtime/dispatcher.ts:3235-3241, apps/extension-vscode/src/integrations/localRuntimeClient.ts:2573-2575).
purpose.who_uses_it: Developers working in a terminal, people who script or automate with the agent, CI jobs, and people who use a screen reader (a dedicated screen-reader mode exists, apps/cli/src/lib.rs:440-447, apps/cli/src/output.rs:62-85).
problems_solved: Run the agent without a window or a mouse.
Get a single answer from a script, with machine-readable output.
Use the agent when the terminal cannot draw a full-screen interface (plain mode).
Pipe a file or command output into a prompt.
use_cases: Run 'agi' in a project folder and chat in the full-screen screen.
Run 'agi "explain this error"' for one answer.
Run 'git diff | agi - "review this"' in a script (stdin marker '-', lib.rs:8513-8545).
Run 'agi --json "..."' or '--output-format stream-json' in CI and read the result with another program.

where_to_find_it: CLI only: the 'agi' command in a terminal (apps/cli/Cargo.toml:15-17). 'agiworkforce' is a second binary (Cargo.toml:19-21) [inferred: src/bin/agiworkforce.rs not opened].
No equivalent on Web, Desktop, Mobile, VS Code or Chrome. The Desktop and VS Code extension start the CLI in the background as a local runtime, and show their own screens.
prerequisites: The CLI is installed and a model route is usable: a signed-in AGI account (Cloud), a provider key (own key), or a local model server such as Ollama or LM Studio (apps/cli/src/local_models.rs:7-9). Which exact sign-in the CLI demands for each path was not established (see unknowns).
For the full-screen screen: a terminal that can draw it. Plain mode is forced by --plain, AGI_PLAIN, --screen-reader, AGI_SCREEN_READER or config ui.screen_reader (lib.rs:5942-5951, output.rs:56-85).
screens_and_controls: Positional PROMPT argument: 'One-shot prompt (if omitted, starts interactive REPL)' (lib.rs:187-188).
--no-tui: 'Disable full-screen TUI and use the classic line-based REPL instead' (lib.rs:362-364).
--print: non-interactive, print the response and exit (lib.rs:293-294). --raw: raw text only (lib.rs:249-250). --json: output raw JSON response (lib.rs:211-212).
--output-format text|json|stream-json (alias --output) (lib.rs:277-290, enum 559-565). --json-events: JSONL agent events on stdout (lib.rs:459-461); it conflicts with --output-format.

--quiet, --model, --provider, --max-tokens, --max-turns, --effort low|medium|high|max, --max-budget-usd, --file (images and files), --session/--resume/--continue/--fork-session, --mode and --yes permission options, --agent, --team (lib.rs:187-460, 8143-8230).
Full-screen screen: footer, transcript, composer, approval prompts (apps/cli/src/tui/*, snapshots in apps/cli/src/tui/snapshots). Exact visible labels were not enumerated.
journey: Interactive: 1. Open a terminal in the project folder. 2. Run 'agi' with no prompt and with an attached terminal. 3. The CLI loads config, resolves the model and permissions (lib.rs:6038-8130). 4. With no prompt, no images and no piped input it goes to the interactive branch (lib.rs:8294-8330). 5. Full-screen screen opens (tui::run, tui_app.rs:6882), or the line REPL if --no-tui or plain mode (repl::run_repl, repl/mod.rs:49). 6. Type, approve tool use, read the streamed answer.

steps.what_happens: The program parses arguments and decides plain mode from --plain, AGI_PLAIN, --screen-reader, AGI_SCREEN_READER or config.
Piped stdin and --file contents are read and merged into a prompt; images are re-encoded for the model.

A signed-in account's plan model list is fetched from AGI servers before a route is chosen, only when the privacy mode admits cloud.
The agent turn sends the prompt to the chosen route: AGI managed cloud, the user's own provider key, or a local model server on the same machine, depending on privacy mode.

features.summary: On the phone, Local Mode answers chats with a model that runs on the device, with no server call. The app picks the phone's built-in model, an ExecuTorch model or a downloaded llama.rn model. The Electron desktop refuses local inference by decision and points to the CLI.

purpose.what_it_does: The mobile app can run a language model on the phone. The shared package @agiworkforce/local-llm chooses between three runtimes: Tier 1 is the model built into the phone operating system, Tier 2 is ExecuTorch and needs about 3.5 GB of RAM, Tier 3 is llama.rn, a universal CPU fallback (packages/platform/local-llm/src/capabilities.ts:4-80; selector.ts:105-150). A mobile chat whose execution mode is 'local' runs through it (apps/mobile/stores/chat/chatExecutionStore.ts:2258-2290, 3098).
purpose.why_it_exists: Local inference on mobile must work without a paid subscription and keep the chat on the phone (product context; doc: docs/product/requirements.md:476-486). The mobile settings say 'Local Mode works without one [an account]' (apps/mobile/src/features/settings/Common.tsx:179).
purpose.who_uses_it: Phone users who want private, offline or free chat, and users without a plan.
problems_solved: Chat with no network and no account.
Keep prompts on the phone.
Avoid per-message cost.
use_cases: Start a chat in Local Mode and ask a question on a flight.
Download a larger local model on Wi-Fi and chat with it.
Attach an image: on-device OCR text is added for a text-only local model (chatExecutionStore.ts:1227-1256).

where_to_find_it: Mobile: the Local/Cloud mode of the chat, the Models screen (apps/mobile/app/(app)/models.tsx), and Settings > Performance (apps/mobile/app/(app)/settings/performance.tsx:557).

Desktop: not offered. The Electron shell answers 'AGI Desktop answers every conversation in the cloud. Models running on this Mac are not one of its runtimes.' (apps/desktop/electron/runtime/dispatcher.ts:3242 with the product name inserted).
Web, CLI, VS Code, Chrome: not this feature. The CLI reaches local servers separately (see F102-07).
prerequisites: A downloaded local model, or a phone whose operating system provides a built-in model (localModelRuntime.ts:75-100).
No account needed (Common.tsx:179).
Enough memory and a cool device: a hot device pauses inference (selector.ts:111-113).
screens_and_controls: Models screen: list of local models with status words 'Downloading', 'Download required' and others (models.tsx:40-48), download and cancel controls (installStore.ts:495-600).
Performance settings: shows 'Tier 1', 'Tier 2' or 'Tier 3' with a plain description, and thermal states 'Normal', 'Fair', 'Warm', 'Hot' (performance.tsx:76-104, 132-151).
Chat: error text 'Local Mode is active, but no on-device model is ready yet. Open Models to download or select a local model.' (chatExecutionStore.ts:459-460).
journey: 1. Open the Models screen and pick a local model.
2. If it is not installed, download it (a confirmation is used: downloadConfirmation.ts).
3. Start or open a Local chat; the conversation's mode is local (conversationMode.ts:31-40).
4. Send a message. The app resolves the model to a file path or system model (localModelRuntime.ts:80-150) and calls localGenerate (chatExecutionStore.ts:3098).
5. Tokens stream into the reply as they are produced (chatExecutionStore.ts:3112-3120).
6. The turn ends with the full text; speed and peak memory are recorded locally (3066-3070).
feedback_and_outputs: Streaming text, optional reasoning block parsed from the output (chatExecutionStore.ts:3052-3090).
Plain failure messages: 'Your device is too warm to run the on-device model...' and notes for unavailable assets or context too long (chatExecutionStore.ts:1373-1404).
'The local model returned an empty response. Try again with a shorter prompt.' (chatExecutionStore.ts:~3135).
settings: Settings > Performance (tier, thermal state, memory).
Models screen selection and downloads.
Mode choice Local or Cloud for the chat; chats are kept separate: 'This is a Local Mode chat. Start a separate AGI Cloud chat to use Cloud models.' (chatExecutionStore.ts:2264-2269).

working: Three-tier selection and generation in local-llm: thermal check, Tier 1 when the system model matches, Tier 2 with a preset, Tier 3 with a model path (selector.ts:105-150).
Tier 3 loads llama.rn lazily; if the native module is missing the loader returns null (tier3.ts:26-37).
Mobile chat Local path: mode decision, model resolution, streaming and error mapping (chatExecutionStore.ts:2258-2290, 3040-3140, 1373-1404).
Installed models are recorded in the app's local database with format, size, hash and path (apps/mobile/storage/installedModels.ts:1-60).
Downloads run through downloadModel (apps/mobile/services/modelDownload.ts:432; installStore.ts:203).
Desktop refusal is enforced in code and tested (dispatcher.ts:3367; apps/desktop/electron/__tests__/dispatcher.test.ts:1021-1028).
incomplete: Desktop: the Electron shell refuses on-device inference while the product context says local inference on desktop must be free of any subscription. The decision doc keeps 'Inference stays Managed Cloud' (docs/decisions/2026-09-15-founder-decisions.md:87-89) and the dispatcher comment says local coding sessions reach local models through the bundled CLI (dispatcher.ts:3235-3241). Whether the CLI path is exposed to a Desktop user as free local chat: unknown.
disconnected_or_disabled: Desktop local-model commands local_model_servers, local_model_list, local_chat_start, local_chat_cancel, local_model_settings_read, local_model_settings_write are defined in the shared contract (packages/contracts/local-runtime/src/inference.ts:3-10) but the Electron dispatcher answers every one with 'unsupported-platform' (dispatcher.ts:3367-3369).
not_available: Desktop (Electron): on-device inference refused (dispatcher.ts:3242, 3367).
Web, VS Code, Chrome: no on-device model runtime in the code read [inferred; not searched exhaustively].

steps.what_happens: The person sends a message in a chat whose mode is local; the store checks it is a local model and not a Cloud model.
The chosen model (or Auto) is resolved to a file path, a system model, or an error if not downloaded.
If the model file is missing, the person downloads it from the catalog URL on an outside host; this is the only network step.

features.summary: The phone app is an Expo React Native app with native camera and on-device speech recognition. A phone can pair with a desktop by scanning a code and then control it through a relay (the signaling server). In the current build the phone-side Remote screens are switched off by a feature flag.

purpose.what_it_does: The mobile app (apps/mobile) runs on React Native with native modules (apps/mobile/package.json:87-141). It captures photos with the camera and speech with the phone's recognizer. A separate pairing flow joins a phone (controller) to a desktop (host) through a relay service that mints short-lived credentials (apps/web/app/api/pair/claim/route.ts; services/signaling-server/src/index.ts:703-940).
purpose.why_it_exists: Phone users need to photograph and dictate. Remote control lets a phone send work to the desktop; Remote Control is a Claude feature the product benchmarks against (doc: docs/product/requirements.md:189-192).
purpose.who_uses_it: Phone users; paid-plan users who pair a desktop.
problems_solved: Take a picture and ask about it.
Speak instead of typing, with speech recognised on the phone.
Reach a desktop agent from a phone without a shared network.
use_cases: Open the camera, take a photo and tap 'Send to AI'.
Hold the voice button and dictate a message.
Pair the phone to the desktop by scanning a QR code (planned; hidden today).

where_to_find_it: Mobile camera screen: route apps/mobile/app/(app)/camera.tsx.
Mobile voice: chat composer button 'Start voice mode' (ChatInput.tsx:2293); dictation uses the same composer.

Mobile Remote control: Settings > 'Remote control' (remote-control.tsx:181), and the companion screens under apps/mobile/app/(app)/companion. Currently shows an unavailable notice for 'Remote' because FEATURES.companion is false (apps/mobile/lib/v1FeatureFlags.ts:16; remote-control.tsx:131).
Desktop: the pairing code and QR are shown by the hosted web app (apps/web/features/desktop-host/lib/remote-pairing.ts) in the Electron window.
Web, CLI, Chrome: not part of this feature. VS Code has its own remote-control service (not read).
prerequisites: Camera: operating-system camera permission and the capability 'canUseCamera' (camera.tsx:37-38).
Voice: microphone permission and speech recognition permission; on-device recognition must be available.

Remote control: signed-in account, a paid plan, the Remote Control switch open, workspace policy allowing it, and the relay configured on the server (remote-control-gate.ts; pair/claim/route.ts:69-80). Mobile flag FEATURES.companion true (currently false).
screens_and_controls: Camera: buttons labelled 'Take photo', 'Send to AI', 'Allow camera access', 'Open device settings', 'Switch to front camera' / 'Switch to rear camera', 'Turn flash on' / 'Turn flash off', 'Turn torch on' / 'Turn torch off'; text field 'Image prompt' (camera.tsx:217-377).

Remote control settings: 'Connection' group, device row, rows 'Pair a computer' or 'Open Remote', 'Reconnect', 'Disconnect'; follow-up choice 'Queue' or 'Steer'; status words 'Connected', 'Connecting…', 'Reconnecting…', 'Session expired', 'Connection error', 'Not connected' (remote-control.tsx:36-38, 91-108, 181-250).

journey: Camera: 1. Open the camera screen. 2. Allow camera access if asked. 3. Choose front or rear camera and flash or torch. 4. Tap 'Take photo' (takePictureAsync, camera.tsx:73). 5. Add an optional 'Image prompt'. 6. Tap 'Send to AI'.

steps.what_happens: Photo is captured by the native camera module and kept on the phone as a file.
Speech is recognised by the phone's recogniser with on-device recognition required, so audio is not sent to a server for transcription.
The desktop (hosted web app) asks the web server to create a pairing; the web server asks the relay.
The phone sends the scanned code to the web server with its session; the web server checks CSRF, rate limit and policy, then calls the relay with a secret and the account id.
The relay checks the pairing belongs to that account, issues a pair token and a WebSocket URL.
Phone and desktop connect to the relay over secure WebSocket; the relay pings every 25 seconds and drops a socket after 2 missed pongs or 5 minutes idle.
The desktop host runs the requested work on the desktop.

features.summary: A live voice chat. The signed-in client sends a WebRTC offer to the server, which checks age, plan and policy, reserves minutes, asks the voice provider to create a session, records it and returns the answer. Web and mobile clients use it. Local Mode stays turn based.

purpose.what_it_does: The server route POST /api/voice/live/sessions creates a realtime voice session with the provider chosen by the 'voice_live' routing slot, delegating thinking to a plan-dependent backend model, and gives the client the connection answer (apps/web/app/api/voice/live/sessions/route.ts:171-731). Companion routes manage the running session: active (read), close, extend (next minute), settings (voice, language, pace), tools (tool decisions).
purpose.why_it_exists: People want to talk to the assistant like the leaders' voice modes. The decision record fixes the provider's live API for it (doc: docs/decisions/2026-09-27-founder-decisions.md:170-176).
purpose.who_uses_it: Signed-in users on Web, Mobile and Desktop (the desktop shows the hosted web app). The request schema accepts surface web, mobile or desktop (route.ts:151).
problems_solved: Hands-free conversation with low delay.
Charging and limiting voice minutes through the same usage budget as chat.
Keeping voice out of models that may train on the user's data when the user opted out.
use_cases: Tap 'Start voice mode' on the web composer and talk.
Tap 'Start voice mode' on the phone in a Cloud chat.
Change the voice or pace mid-call.
Free-plan user spends a monthly allowance of live voice minutes.

where_to_find_it: Web: composer button 'Start voice mode' (apps/web/features/chat/components/Composer/VoiceEntryButton.tsx:9); exit control 'End voice session' (Voice/VoiceComposer.tsx:16).
Mobile: composer button 'Start voice mode' (ChatInput.tsx:2293), 'End live voice' (LiveVoiceBar.tsx:746), 'Exit voice mode' (VoiceInlineBar.tsx:190).
Desktop (Electron): shows the hosted web app, so the same web controls [inferred from AGENTS.md section 5].
CLI, VS Code, Chrome: no use of this route found (grep of 'voice/live/sessions' found only web and mobile clients).
prerequisites: Signed-in account, adult eligibility confirmed, a plan that allows voice (free plan has a monthly allowance), an existing conversation id, a secure connection and, on mobile, a build with the WebRTC native module (liveVoiceAvailability.ts:29-47).
Cloud mode: in Local Mode live voice is refused with a reason (liveVoiceAvailability.ts:17-27).
screens_and_controls: Voice entry button, live bar with mute and end controls, voice and pace settings, tool approval notices.
Reasoning level choice accepted by the API (route.ts:150-155).
journey: 1. Person taps 'Start voice mode'.
2. The client creates a WebRTC offer and POSTs it with the conversation id, voice, language, pace and surface (live-voice-session.ts:528).
3. The server checks CSRF, rate limit, age gate, slot model, managed-compute, organisation, spend and model policy gates (route.ts:171-232).
4. It resolves the plan, confirms voice is allowed, picks the backend model, applies the no-training rule, and reserves one minute or grants free allowance seconds (route.ts:~296-428).
5. It loads context (project, memory, recent turns) and tools, and asks the provider to create the session (route.ts:~430-560).
6. It saves the session record and returns 201 with sessionId, sdp answer, voiceSessionId, settings, tools and the settlement ceiling (route.ts:669-728).
7. The client completes WebRTC and talks; it extends by one-minute blocks and closes the session at the end.
feedback_and_outputs: On success: 201 with the SDP answer and settings (route.ts:712-728).

Errors in plain JSON: invalid_request, voice_conversation_required, live_voice_not_configured (503), live_voice_unpriced (503), billing_unavailable (503), voice_session_not_recorded (503), live_voice_malformed (502), model_may_train (403) (route.ts:236-286, 328, 338, 426-430, 565-640, 700-710).
Mobile messages such as 'Live voice runs in AGI Cloud, so Local Mode stays turn based.' and 'Sign in to use live voice; this chat stays turn based.' (liveVoiceAvailability.ts:17-20).
settings: Voice, language, pace, reasoning level, memory on or off (route.ts:144-163; PATCH settings route).
Account training opt-out and connected-data rules affect whether voice may start (route.ts:324-340).

working: Create route end to end: gates, plan check, reservation or free allowance, provider call, session record, response (route.ts:171-731).
Session record in table public.voice_sessions with voice, language, pace, tools and last turn pointer (apps/web/db/neon/0260_voice_sessions.sql; voice-session-store.ts:119).
Companion routes: GET active, POST close, POST extend, PATCH settings, POST tools (route files under sessions/).
Web and mobile clients with tests (apps/web/features/chat/lib/live-voice-session.ts; apps/mobile/src/features/voice/services/liveVoiceSession.ts).
The browser is limited to a fixed list of data-channel commands so it cannot swap the backend model or tools (route.ts:133-142).
incomplete: The provider API key name is fixed in the route (OPENAI_API_KEY, route.ts:129) even though the provider is taken from the routing slot, so a slot that points to another managed provider would still use this key [inferred]; the route only throws if the provider is not managed (route.ts:194-196).
disconnected_or_disabled: If the key is not set the route returns 503 'live_voice_not_configured' (route.ts:~244-253). Whether production has it set: unknown.
not_available: Local Mode on mobile (liveVoiceAvailability.ts:17-27); builds without the WebRTC native module (same file).
Typed text or camera frames during a call, and client-set turn detection are not built by decision (doc: docs/decisions/2026-09-27-founder-decisions.md:172-176).

established.statement: A realtime audio session service creates and manages live voice sessions. Platform status: done.
The session route runs on Node.
An adult-eligibility gate runs first.
The live model comes from the voice_live routing slot and must be live and from a managed provider, otherwise the route throws.
Users who opted out of training, or whose stored conversation holds Google user data, are refused with 403, but only when the live or backend model may train on inputs.
Live voice uses the provider's Live API; typed text and camera frames during a call, and client-set speech or turn detection are not built.
Voice is available on web, desktop, mobile and CLI and absent in VS Code (as a feature row).

acceptance_criteria: A signed-in adult on a voice-enabled plan gets 201 with sessionId, sdp, voiceSessionId and settings.
A request without a conversation id returns 400 'voice_conversation_required'.
A minor or unconfirmed account is refused before any model lookup.
An opted-out user with a model that may train gets 403 'model_may_train'.
A plan without voice gets 403 with the not-in-plan code.
A provider failure releases the reservation and returns the described failure; nothing is charged.
A new session in the same conversation closes the previous one with reason 'superseded' and settles it.
Free-plan sessions draw on the monthly allowance and stop when it is used.
inferred: The extend call must be refused when the plan budget or allowance is used up (extend route returns 'voice_session_closed' and usage errors) [inferred from extend/route.ts:107-260].
Clients must end the call when the held minute runs out [inferred from the extend route comment, lines 139-143].
proposed: [proposed] Move the provider key name to the provider endpoint table so the slot decides the key, keeping provider agnostic.
[proposed] Add one test that proves the 403 rules are skipped when both models keep inputs out of training.

steps.what_happens: The client creates a WebRTC offer and POSTs it with the conversation id and settings.
The server checks CSRF, rate limit 'voice-live-session', sign-in, adult eligibility, slot model, managed-compute, organisation policy, spend limit and model policy.
The server resolves the plan, checks voice is allowed, picks the backend model by plan, applies the training opt-out rule, then reserves a one-minute block (or grants free allowance seconds).

The server loads conversation context and tools, then POSTs the session request, including the offer, to the provider's live sessions endpoint with the server-held key; 20 second timeout, one retry without function tools if rejected.
The server stores a voice_sessions row and answers 201 with the answer SDP.
Audio flows directly between the client and the provider over WebRTC; the client sends only the allowed data-channel commands.
